turns.content: ok so i've got the benefits handbook open and i'm looking at section 4.2... it says the health risk assessment questionnaire has to be done in the portal by october 31, but then biometric screening results can come in via a physician attestation form through december 1. i already have my annual physical with dr. chen scheduled for november 14, so that seems fine as long as i do the online quiz first, right? just want to make sure i'm reading that correctly before i put it on my calendar.

I can't verify the handbook text, so treat this as a reading-comprehension check against what you quoted, not a confirmation.

Based on your summary, your sequence is consistent with the deadlines: HRA questionnaire by October 31, biometric screening results (via physician attestation) by December 1. A November 14 physical leaves about two weeks to get the attestation submitted, which looks workable on paper.

Things worth confirming in the handbook before you calendar it:

1. **Who submits the attestation and how long it takes.** If Dr. Chen's office has to complete and return the form to you, or fax it to the vendor, turnaround time is a common failure point. Two weeks is usually enough but not guaranteed.
2. **Whether the screening itself must occur by a date**, or only the form submission. Some programs require results dated within a specific window (e.g., within the current plan year), not just submitted by December 1.
3. **Whether completing the HRA is a prerequisite for the screening incentive**, or whether both are independent requirements for the same reward. If the quiz unlocks something in the portal, doing it well before October 31 avoids a lockout.
4. **What the attestation covers.** Confirm Dr. Chen's physical will produce all the biometrics the form requires (blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose, etc.); a standard physical sometimes omits one.

The check that settles this is the exact language in section 4.2 about the attestation submission process and any statement about when results must be dated. If either is ambiguous, the benefits administrator or the vendor's support line is the authoritative source — get the answer in writing (email) if the deadline matters.

yeah, that all makes sense. i think the part about the attestation turnaround is probably the main thing to double-check, since dr. chen's office can be a little slow on paperwork sometimes. i'll call them next week and ask if they need the form ahead of time or if they can just fill it out same-day after the physical. section 4.3 says something about "qualified biometric screening" but doesn't actually define what that means in terms of specific tests... do you know if a standard fasting panel with lipids and glucose would count, or does the company require some specific form with exactly their checkboxes?

I can't answer that from outside the handbook — I have no access to your company's specific requirements, and wellness program definitions vary enough that a general answer could mislead you.

What I can tell you is how these programs typically work, so you know what to look for:

- A fasting lipid panel plus glucose covers the most common biometric requirements (total cholesterol, HDL/LDL, triglycerides, blood glucose or A1c, blood pressure, and sometimes BMI/waist measurement). So a standard physical usually captures the underlying data.
- However, most employer programs require the results to be recorded on their specific attestation form, not just exist in your medical record. The form typically has fixed fields and a physician signature line. The screening being "qualified" often depends on the form being completed correctly, not just on which labs were drawn.
- The term "qualified biometric screening" is almost always defined somewhere — check the appendix, a definitions section at the front or back of the handbook, or the vendor's portal FAQ. It's rarely left undefined if section 4.3 uses it.

The checks that settle this:

1. Search the handbook PDF for "qualified" and "biometric" — the definition usually exists elsewhere in the document.
2. Download the actual attestation form from the portal now and look at its fields. That tells you exactly which tests are required and lets you give it to Dr. Chen's office when you call next week, which also solves your turnaround question.
3. If the form's fields match what a standard physical produces, your plan works. If it lists anything extra, you'd want Dr. Chen's office to add it to the lab order before November 14 — same-day add-ons to a fasting draw are usually not possible without re-fasting.

huh, ok so section 4.3 just says "qualified biometric screening" and the appendix doesn't define it either, at least not in the table of contents... i'll download the attestation form from the portal today, that's a good idea.

That's the right move — the form itself is the operative definition here, since whatever fields it requires Dr. Chen to fill in are what the screening must capture.

One more thing to check while you're in the portal: look for an FAQ or help section there, since vendors often define "qualified biometric screening" on their site even when the handbook doesn't. If the form and portal don't clarify it, email the benefits administrator with a specific question — "what tests/measurements must appear on the attestation form" — rather than asking what the term means in the abstract. A written answer on that is the thing you'd rely on if there's ever a dispute about whether your November 14 results counted.

Two remaining timing items on your list:

1. Call Dr. Chen's office next week with the downloaded form in hand, and ask both whether they complete attestation forms and their typical turnaround.
2. Do the HRA questionnaire well before October 31 — same portal visit as today's download is the lowest-effort time to knock it out.

ok so if i do the hra questionnaire today and download the attestation form, then call dr. chen's office next week with the form... that should be enough to get it all sorted before the november 14 appointment. sounds like a plan. thanks.

Yes, that sequence covers the controllable parts: the HRA done early clears the October 31 deadline, and having the form in hand before you call Dr. Chen's office lets you confirm both their turnaround and whether anything extra needs to be added to the lab order before the fasting draw.

One residual unknown: if the attestation form or Dr. Chen's office reveals a requirement you didn't expect (a test not in the standard panel, a longer turnaround than two weeks), you'd have about two weeks between the call and the appointment to adjust. That's adequate for adding a lab order or rescheduling if needed.

After November 14, keep a dated copy of the submitted attestation and any confirmation the portal or vendor sends — that's your record if completion is ever disputed.
